Nigeria has risen seven places to 11th in RMB’s 2026/27 Where to Invest in Africa report, marking the largest movement in this year’s rankings and indicating that recent economic reforms are strengthening the country’s investment outlook. The improvement follows a period of significant adjustment. Nigeria ranked 9th in 2024/25 before falling to 18th in 2025/26 as the economy absorbed the short-term impact of key reforms. Its rise to 11th points to improving stability, although structural challenges linger. “Last year’s decline was the immediate reaction to necessary long-term reform. Nigeria’s improved position now reflects the view that the economy has been set on a more stable course. Good policy decisions are hard to make and implement, but they ultimately drive investment and economic growth,” says Isaah Mhlanga, Chief Economist at RMB. Attractiveness today, durability tomorrow The report highlights the importance of viewing Nigeria’s performance over time. While the latest ranking signals progress, it also reflects policy reforms, foreign-exchange market changes and statistical updates, including GDP and CPI rebasing. RMB’s new Resilience and Vulnerability Matrix provides additional insight into the sustainability of investment opportunities. Beyond asking which markets are attractive today, it considers which are building opportunities that can endure pressure. Resilience refers to the policies, institutions and buffers that help an economy withstand and recover from shocks. Vulnerability captures structural exposure, such as export concentration, import dependence, climate risk and external financing needs. Make PUNCH part of your everyday experience. However, structural factors relating to public institutions, economic complexity and oil dependence continue to influence Nigeria’s long-term resilience profile. The report identifies macroeconomic stability as a relative strength, while strength of public institutions remains the country’s largest gap. Turning reform into durable investment momentum “Investment attractiveness is not only about current opportunities, but also about the ability to sustain progress through periods of volatility,” says Mhlanga. The report concludes that Nigeria’s stronger ranking is an early indication that reforms are beginning to improve the investment trajectory. Sustaining this progress will depend on continued reform implementation, stronger public institutions, greater economic diversification and reduced structural vulnerabilities.
